Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: A systematic review of mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes among survivors of hantavirus infection
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infections, including hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, can cause severe acute illness. Although survival has improved in some clinical settings, the mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes associated with recovery remain insufficiently characterized. This systematic review synthesized the available evidence on mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes associated with hantavirus infection, distinguishing persistent post-infectious symptoms from neurological complications occurring during acute illness. A systematic review was conducted with reference to PRISMA 2020 guidance. Electronic databases were searched for eligible studies published between 2005 and 2025. Methodological quality was evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools, and findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, follow-up periods, and outcome assessment. Nine studies were included. Reported outcomes fell into two broad clinical categories. The first comprised persistent or follow-up symptoms, including fatigue, memory and concentration difficulties, psychological symptoms, sleep disturbances, and impaired quality of life. These outcomes were described in studies examining recovery after HCPS and Puumala virus-associated nephropathia epidemica. The second category comprised neurological complications, including encephalitis, altered mental status, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. These acute manifestations were interpreted separately from persistent post-infectious outcomes because their occurrence during acute illness does not establish long-term neuropsychiatric impairment. Differences in study design, sample size, follow-up duration, and outcome assessment limited direct comparisons and prevented reliable estimates of population-level prevalence. The available literature describes a range of persistent symptoms and acute neurological complications associated with hantavirus infection. However, the small and heterogeneous evidence base limits conclusions regarding their frequency, duration, mechanisms, and functional consequences. Larger longitudinal studies using standardized assessments and appropriate comparison groups are needed to clarify recovery trajectories and inform follow-up care.

full_text_sections.full_text: A systematic review of mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes among survivors of hantavirus infection All claims expressed in this article are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of their affiliated organizations, or those of the publisher, the editors and the reviewers. Any product that may be evaluated in this article or claim that may be made by its manufacturer is not guaranteed or endorsed by the publisher. Accepted: 15 November 2026 Published: 26 November 2026 Hantavirus infections, including hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, can cause severe acute illness. Although survival has improved in some clinical settings, the mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes associated with recovery remain insufficiently characterized. This systematic review synthesized the available evidence on mental health and neuropsychiatric outcomes associated with hantavirus infection, distinguishing persistent post-infectious symptoms from neurological complications occurring during acute illness. A systematic review was conducted with reference to PRISMA 2020 guidance. Electronic databases were searched for eligible studies published between 2005 and 2025. Methodological quality was evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools, and findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, follow-up periods, and outcome assessment. Nine studies were included. Reported outcomes fell into two broad clinical categories. The first comprised persistent or follow-up symptoms, including fatigue, memory and concentration difficulties, psychological symptoms, sleep disturbances, and impaired quality of life. These outcomes were described in studies examining recovery after HCPS and Puumala virus-associated nephropathia epidemica. The second category comprised neurological complications, including encephalitis, altered mental status, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. These acute manifestations were interpreted separately from persistent post-infectious outcomes because their occurrence during acute illness does not establish long-term neuropsychiatric impairment. Differences in study design, sample size, follow-up duration, and outcome assessment limited direct comparisons and prevented reliable estimates of population-level prevalence. The available literature describes a range of persistent symptoms and acute neurological complications associated with hantavirus infection. However, the small and heterogeneous evidence base limits conclusions regarding their frequency, duration, mechanisms, and functional consequences. Larger longitudinal studies using standardized assessments and appropriate comparison groups are needed to clarify recovery trajectories and inform follow-up care. analysis.background: Hantavirus infections such as HCPS and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome cause severe acute illness, yet the mental health and neuropsychiatric sequelae after survival are poorly described (A1, A2).
analysis.main_directions: The review categorises outcomes into persistent post‑infectious symptoms (fatigue, cognitive deficits, psychological distress, sleep problems, reduced quality of life) and acute neurological complications (encephalitis, altered mental status, PRES) (A9, A11).
analysis.current_state: Nine heterogeneous studies were identified and narratively synthesized, revealing a range of persistent and acute neuropsychiatric manifestations but providing no reliable prevalence estimates (A3, A6, A7, A13, A14).
analysis.gaps: Small sample sizes, varied designs, inconsistent follow‑up periods, and non‑standardized outcome measures prevent firm conclusions about frequency, duration, mechanisms, and functional impact (A13, A15, A17).
analysis.future_research: Large, longitudinal cohort studies with standardized neuropsychiatric assessments and appropriate control groups are required to define recovery trajectories and guide follow‑up care (A16, A18).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause severe acute disease, but post‑recovery mental health outcomes are understudied (A1, A2). Main directions: Outcomes fall into persistent symptoms (fatigue, cognition, mood, sleep, quality of life) and acute neurological events (encephalitis, altered mental status, PRES) (A9, A11). Current state: Nine heterogeneous studies were narratively reviewed, showing diverse manifestations but no solid prevalence data (A3, A6, A7, A13, A14). Gaps: Limited sample sizes, heterogeneity, and non‑standard assessments hinder understanding of frequency, mechanisms, and impact (A13, A15, A17). Future research: Conduct large longitudinal studies with standardized tools and comparison groups to map recovery trajectories and inform care (A16, A18).

analysis_zh.gaps: 样本量小、研究设计多样、随访时间不一致以及结果测量未标准化,阻碍了对频率、持续时间、机制和功能影响的明确结论 (A13, A15, A17)。

papers.title: Cardiovascular Involvement in Hantavirus Infection-Pathophysiology, Clinical Manifestations, and Management
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection can lead to hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and cardiovascular (CV) involvement is increasingly recognized as an important feature of severe disease. The present review summarizes the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic evaluation, and management of CV involvement in hantavirus infection. The available evidence includes experimental studies, observational cohorts, case series, and clinical reports. Reported CV manifestations include myocardial injury, myocarditis, ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, pericardial involvement, conduction abnormalities, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, increased vascular permeability, inflammatory and cytokine activation, autonomic nervous system dysregulation, and microvascular abnormalities. Clinical assessment may reveal hypotension, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ventricular dysfunction, and circulatory collapse. Echocardiography, cardiac biomarker assessment, electrocardiography, speckle-tracking echocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may aid diagnosis and risk stratification. Management is largely supportive and may include individualized fluid management, vasopressors and inotropes as needed, hemodynamic monitoring, and mechanical circulatory support or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for refractory shock. The current evidence base is limited by the predominance of observational data and heterogeneity in diagnostic and follow-up strategies. Prospective studies are needed to clarify the mechanisms of myocardial injury, identify prognostic biomarkers, and establish evidence-based approaches to CV assessment and management.

papers.full_text: Abstract Host classification from viral genomic sequences is challenging because biologically meaningful signals must be extracted from high-dimensional sequence data under strong class imbalance. This paper presents a hybrid quantum machine learning framework for binary human versus non-human host classification. Raw nucleotide sequences are first encoded using a frozen DNABERT-2 model and compressed into bounded low-dimensional latent vectors through a bottleneck autoencoder. These quantum-compatible features are then classified using the proposed Segment-Aware Entangled Quantum Classifier (SEQC), a compact variational quantum decision module with trainable dual-angle encoding, data re-uploading, segment-aware local-to-global entanglement, global mixing, and trainable observable readout. Experiments are conducted in a leakage-safe, resource-controlled simulation setting: classifier training uses a balanced subset of samples, while validation, threshold tuning, and testing are performed on the full natural imbalanced splits. On the natural test set, SEQC achieves \(0.8833\) accuracy, \(0.7224\) balanced accuracy, \(0.7243\) macro-F1, \(0.7740\) ROC-AUC, and \(0.5167\) minority-class PR-AUC using only \(138\) trainable classifier parameters. Comparisons with classical baselines show that SEQC is competitive as a compact nonlinear decision module, particularly in minority-class ranking. Ablation studies further indicate that encoding choice, bottleneck dimension, and entanglement structure should be matched to the supplied latent representation. analysis_zh.background: 从病毒基因组序列进行宿主分类具有挑战性,因为必须在强类别不平衡的高维数据中提取生物学意义的信号 (F1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究提出了一种用于二分类(人类 vs 非人类宿主)预测的混合量子机器学习框架 (F2);原始核苷酸序列使用冻结的 DNABERT‐2 模型进行编码,并通过瓶颈自编码器进行压缩 (F3);得到的低维向量由段感知纠缠量子分类器 (SEQC) 分类,该分类器是具备双角度编码、数据重新上传、段感知纠缠和可训练读出层的变分量子决策模块 (F4);训练使用平衡子集,而在完整的自然不平衡划分上进行验证、阈值调优和测试,采用防泄漏仿真 (F5)。
analysis_zh.results: 在自然测试集上,SEQC 仅使用 138 个可训练分类器参数即可达到 0.8833 的准确率、0.7224 的平衡准确率、0.7243 的宏 F1、0.7740 的 ROC‐AUC 和 0.5167 的少数类 PR‐AUC (F6);对比结果表明其在少数类排序方面尤其能够与经典基线竞争 (F7)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作提出了一种紧凑的量子分类器,在不平衡宿主预测任务中能够与经典方法竞争,凸显其在高效少数类排序方面的潜力 (F7)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告局限性;描述基于摘要和部分文本,因而缺乏详细的实验或硬件约束信息。

papers.title: Hantavirus Transmission Dynamics in the United States: Reservoir Ecology, Environmental and Social Drivers, and Public Health Implications
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is a rare but severe rodent-borne zoonosis. As of the end of 2023, the United States had recorded 890 laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases since surveillance began in 1993, with 35% case fatality and 94% of cases west of the Mississippi River. This narrative review, searched through November 2026, synthesises epidemiological surveillance, reservoir ecology, ecological niche modelling, social-vulnerability analyses, and climate research to explain where and why Sin Nombre virus (SNV) spills over to people. We integrate evidence that SNV is detected in, and infectious virus isolated from, several rodent species beyond the western deer mouse (Peromyscus sonoriensis, formerly P. maniculatus), though independent maintenance is unproven; niche models linking suitability to arid climates and low-intensity development; the 2025 clusters in New Mexico and California; Seoul virus infections linked to pet rats; and the 2026 Andes virus outbreak on a cruise ship, which renewed attention to person-to-person-transmissible hantaviruses. We separate well-established findings from tentative, correlational inferences about biodiversity, social vulnerability, and climate change, and summarise clinical recognition and management. Priorities include taxonomy-aware rodent surveillance, integrated One Health forecasting, diagnosis and referral to centres offering extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and targeted prevention for rural, Indigenous, and occupationally exposed communities.

analysis.background: HPS is a rare but severe rodent‑borne zoonosis in the United States. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review integrates surveillance, reservoir ecology, ecological niche modelling, social‑vulnerability and climate research to explain where and why Sin Nombre virus spills over to people. (A3)
analysis.current_state: Since 1993 the US has recorded 890 laboratory‑confirmed hantavirus cases (35% fatality), 94% west of the Mississippi, with recent 2025 clusters in New Mexico and California, detection of SNV in multiple rodent species, niche models linking suitability to arid climates and low‑intensity development, Seoul virus infections linked to pet rats, and a 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak. (A2,A5,A6,A7,A8)
analysis.gaps: Independent maintenance of SNV in non‑deer‑mouse hosts is unproven, and many associations with biodiversity, social vulnerability and climate change remain tentative and correlational. (A4,A10)
analysis.future_research: Priorities include taxonomy‑aware rodent surveillance, integrated One Health forecasting, improved diagnosis and ECMO referral, and targeted prevention for rural, Indigenous and occupationally exposed communities. (A11)

analysis.summary_en: Background: HPS is a rare but severe rodent‑borne zoonosis in the US. Main directions: The review integrates surveillance, reservoir ecology, niche modelling, social‑vulnerability and climate analyses to explain SNV spillover. Current state: Since 1993, 890 confirmed cases (35% fatality) have occurred, mostly west of the Mississippi, with recent NM and CA clusters, SNV detection in multiple rodents, niche models linking risk to arid, low‑intensity development, Seoul virus from pet rats, and a 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak. Gaps: Independent maintenance of SNV in non‑deer‑mouse hosts is unproven and many biodiversity‑social‑climate links are tentative. Future research: Priorities are taxonomy‑aware rodent surveillance, One Health forecasting, better diagnosis and ECMO referral, and targeted prevention for rural, Indigenous and occupationally exposed groups.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 美国传播动力学:储宿主生态、环境与社会驱动因素及公共卫生影响

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征是一种罕见但严重的啮齿动物传播的人畜共患病,发生于美国。(A1)
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述整合了监测、宿主生态、生态位模型、社会脆弱性和气候研究,以阐明Sin Nombre病毒向人类溢出的地点和原因。(A3)
analysis_zh.current_state: 自1993年以来,美国已记录了890例实验室确诊的汉坦病毒病例(致死率35%),其中94%位于密西西比河以西;近期2025年在新墨西哥州和加利福尼亚州出现聚集病例;在多种啮齿动物中检测到SNV;生态位模型将适宜性与干旱气候和低强度开发关联;首尔病毒感染与宠物鼠有关;以及2026年发生的安第斯病毒邮轮暴发。(A2,A5,A6,A7,A8)
analysis_zh.gaps: SNV在非鹿鼠宿主中的独立维持尚未得到证实,且许多与生物多样性、社会脆弱性和气候变化的关联仍属暂时性和相关性。(A4,A10)
analysis_zh.future_research: 优先事项包括具备分类学意识的啮齿动物监测、综合One Health预测、改进的诊断和ECMO转诊,以及针对农村、原住民和职业暴露社区的精准防控。(A11)

Hantavirus Infection: A Comprehensive Review of Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Prevention Sowmya Santhanam and Sharanya Krishnakumar* Department of Microbiology, Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, Bharath Institute of Higher Education and Research, Chennai-600044, Tamil Nadu, India Received: July 27, 2026 / Accepted: August 28, 2026 / Published: November 24, 2026 Introduction Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose a sub- stantial challenge to global public health, particularly when ecological, climatic, and socioeconomic changes alter the interactions between humans, animals, and their environments. Urbanization, climate variability, deforestation, land-use change, and increasing human– animal contact can modify rodent population dynamics and expand opportunities for zoonotic transmission. However, the occurrence of hantavirus infection cannot be attributed to any single environmental factor; rather, it reflects the complex interaction between reservoir ecology, viral characteristics, human behavior, and envi- Hantavirus infection is a globally important zoonosis caused by viruses of the family Hantaviridae, maintained predominantly in rodent reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through exposure to contaminated excreta. Ecological disruption, climate variability, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urbanization, and increasing human–animal interactions can modify reservoir dynamics and create opportunities for zoonotic spillover. Depending on the infecting virus, disease ranges from hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) to severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Disease severity is primarily associated with endothelial dysfunction, increased vascular permeability, immune dysregulation, and cytokine-mediated inflammation. Diagnosis remains challenging because early manifestations are nonspecific and overlap with other endemic febrile illnesses. Serological methods, particularly enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays, remain central to routine diagnosis, while RT-qPCR provides valuable early-phase detection. Emerging approaches, including RT-LAMP, digital PCR, next-generation sequencing, metagenomic sequencing, and CRISPR-based assays, offer opportunities for rapid detection and genomic characterization, although cost, infrastructure, standardization, and clinical validation remain limitations. Treatment is predominantly supportive, with ribavirin showing potential benefit when administered early in selected HFRS cases, while favipiravir, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed therapies remain investigational. Vaccine development using inactivated, DNA, viral-vector, and mRNA platforms has progressed, but broad and durable protection remains an unmet need. This review critically examines epidemiology, reservoir ecology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnostic advances, therapeutic strategies, vaccine development, prevention, and One Health surveillance. Emphasis is placed on affordable diagnostics, genomic surveillance, early risk prediction, and scalable preventive strategies to strengthen preparedness and reduce the global burden of hantavirus disease. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 ronmental conditions [1]. This complexity makes predic- tion and prevention of hantavirus outbreaks particularly challenging. Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae. They are maintained predominantly in specific rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs, with individual virus–host associations contributing to distinct geographic and clinical patterns. Human infection generally occurs following inhalation or other exposure to virus-containing rodent excreta or contaminated environmental materials [2]. Although human-to-human transmission is uncommon for most hantaviruses, the ability of these viruses to produce severe disease follow- ing relatively infrequent zoonotic spillover makes them an important public health concern. Thus, the epidemio- logical significance of hantaviruses is determined not only by their geographic distribution but also by the ecological conditions that bring infected reservoirs and susceptible human populations into contact [3]. The clinical importance of hantaviruses became apparent with the recognition of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), historically described as Korean hemorrhagic fever, and the subsequent isolation of Han- taan virus in 1978. The discovery of Sin Nombre virus during the 1993 outbreak in the Four Corners region of the United States further expanded the clinical spectrum of hantavirus disease and established hantavirus cardio- pulmonary syndrome (HCPS) as a severe respiratory manifestation associated with high mortality. These discoveries demonstrated that hantavirus disease is not a single clinical entity but a spectrum of syndromes influenced by viral genotype, reservoir host, geographic distribution, and host response. Despite considerable advances in molecular epidemiology, serological diagnosis, molecular detection, genomic sequencing, and supportive clinical management, important challenges remain unresolved [4]. Early diagnosis is complicated by non- specific initial clinical manifestations and the narrow window during which viral RNA may be detectable, whereas serological assays may be influenced by assay design, antigen selection, and the timing of antibody development. Similarly, advanced approaches such as digital PCR, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and CRISPR-based diagnostics offer potential advantages but remain constrained by cost, infrastructure, technical expertise, assay standardization, and limited clinical validation. Consequently, the most technologically advanced diagnostic approach is not necessarily the most appropriate for routine use, particularly in resource- limited endemic settings [5]. Therapeutic options also remain limited. Management continues to rely predomi- nantly on early recognition, intensive supportive care, and organ-specific management, while antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed therapies remain at different stages of investigation. Likewise, the development of broadly protective vaccines is complicated by the genetic and antigenic diversity of hantaviruses and their geographically restricted reservoir associations. These limitations highlight an important gap between technological progress and its translation into accessible clinical and public-health interventions [6]. Against this background, an updated assessment of hantavirus infection should extend beyond a description of established knowledge. A critical evaluation is needed to compare diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, identify limitations in current evidence, examine the feasibility of emerging technologies, and define priorities for sur- veillance, prevention, and vaccine development. This review therefore examines the current understanding of hantavirus virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, therapeutic strate- gies, prevention, and One Health surveillance, while critically considering unresolved questions, implementa- tion barriers, and future research priorities [7]. Virology Hantaviruses are enveloped, spherical viruses belong- ing to the family Hantaviridae, with virions measuring approximately 80–120 nm in diameter. The viral envelope is derived from the host-cell membrane and contains two surface glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which mediate receptor interaction, cellular attachment, membrane fusion, and viral entry. The genome comprises three segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA: the Large (L) segment, which encodes the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) responsible for viral transcription and replication; the Medium (M) segment, which encodes the precursor of the envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc; and the Small (S) segment, which encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein [8]. The N protein is involved not only in encapsidation of the viral genome but also in viral replica- tion, assembly, and modulation of host-cell responses. Hantaviruses exhibit considerable genetic and ecological Microbiol. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 3 diversity, with distinct virus-reservoir associations con- tributing to differences in geographic distribution, epide- miology, and clinical disease. Traditionally, hantaviruses associated with HFRS in Asia and Europe have been referred to as Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), Puumala virus (PUUV), and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), whereas viruses associated predominantly with HCPS in the Americas have been classified as New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Andes virus (ANDV), Laguna Negra virus, and Black Creek Canal virus. Although this geographical classification remains useful from a clinical and epidemiological perspective, it rep- resents a broad framework rather than a strict biologi- cal division, as hantavirus diversity is closely linked to specific reservoir hosts and evolutionary relationships [9]. The relationship between viral genotype, reservoir host, and clinical phenotype is particularly important in understanding disease severity. Old World hantaviruses are predominantly associated with HFRS, whereas several New World hantaviruses are associated with HCPS, characterized by pulmonary capillary leakage, acute respiratory deterioration, and substantial mortality [10]. However, clinical outcome is not determined solely by viral classification and is also influenced by host immune responses, viral factors, and the timing and quality of clinical management. Andes virus is of particular epidemiological interest because person-to-person trans- mission has been well documented, primarily among close contacts in South America, distinguishing it from the transmission patterns observed with most other pathogenic hantaviruses [11]. This observation high- lights the importance of considering virus-specific trans- mission characteristics when developing surveillance, infection-control, and outbreak-response strategies. Epidemiology, Reservoirs, and Transmission Hantavirus epidemiology is closely linked to the dis- tribution and ecology of its small-mammal reservoirs. Although individual hantaviruses generally show strong virus–host associations, the presence of a reservoir species alone does not necessarily result in human disease. Transmission depends on reservoir abundance and infection prevalence, environmental conditions, human behavior, and the frequency of contact between infected animals and susceptible populations. HFRS is predominantly reported in Asia and Europe, with China accounting for a substantial proportion of reported cases, while Puumala virus is the major cause of nephropathia epidemica in Europe. In the Americas, hantavirus infec- tion is primarily associated with HCPS, which generally has a more severe clinical course and higher case-fatality than HFRS [12]. However, regional differences in reported incidence and mortality may reflect not only viral characteristics but also variations in surveillance, diagnostic capacity, early recognition, and access to intensive care. This highlights the importance of inter- preting epidemiological estimates within their healthcare and surveillance context. Important reservoir associations include Apodemus agrarius with Hantaan virus, Myodes glareolus with Puumala virus, Peromyscus maniculatus with Sin Nombre virus, and Sigmodon hispidus with Black Creek Canal virus [13]. These associations con- tribute to the characteristic geographic distribution of hantaviruses, while changes in reservoir population density, habitat, and distribution can influence the temporal and spatial risk of human infection. Human infection most commonly follows inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with rodent urine, feces, saliva, or nesting materials. Direct contact with contaminated materials and, less frequently, rodent bites may also result in transmission. Occupational and recreational activities—including agriculture, forestry, military activities, cleaning rodent-infested buildings, camping, and other outdoor exposures—can increase the likeli- hood of contact with infected rodents [14]. Environmental and climatic factors may further modify transmission by influencing rodent abundance and food availability. However, these relationships vary geographically, mak- ing climate alone insufficient for reliable outbreak predic- tion. Integrating environmental monitoring with rodent surveillance and human epidemiological data may provide a more informative assessment of transmission risk. Andes virus is an important exception to the pre- dominantly zoonotic transmission pattern, as person-to- person transmission has been documented, particularly following prolonged and close contact [15]. This virus- specific characteristic has implications for outbreak investigation and infection-control measures and should not be generalized to other hantaviruses. Although hantavirus antibodies have been detected in several domestic and wild animals, serological evidence alone does not establish reservoir competence. Rodents there- fore remain the principal recognized reservoirs of medically 4 Microbiol. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 important hantaviruses. Overall, hantavirus trans- mission is best understood through a reservoir–virus– environment–human framework, supporting the need for integrated One Health surveillance that combines rodent ecology, environmental monitoring, molecular epidemiology, and human disease surveillance [16]. Pathogenesis and Clinical Manifestations The hallmark of hantavirus disease is increased vascular permeability resulting primarily from endothelial dysfunction rather than extensive direct cytopathic injury. Following exposure to virus-contaminated rodent excreta, hantaviruses infect endothelial and immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells. Viral entry involves interactions with cellular receptors, including β3 integrins expressed on endothelial cells. Viral replication and the subsequent interaction between infected cells and the host immune system initiate a complex inflammatory response involving cytokines, chemokines, complement activation, and cellular immune mechanisms [17]. Rather than being explained by viral replication alone, vascular leakage appears to result from the combined effects of altered endothelial-cell function and an exaggerated host immune response. Increased levels of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL- 1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), have been associated with endothelial activation and increased vascular permeability. Complement activation and cytotoxic T-cell responses may further influence disease progression. Although cellular immunity is important for controlling viral infection, an excessive or dysregulated immune response may contribute to endo- thelial dysfunction and tissue injury [18]. Thus, disease severity is likely determined by the interaction between viral characteristics, host immune responses, and the extent of endothelial barrier disruption rather than by direct viral cytotoxicity alone. The resulting capillary-leak syndrome provides a com- mon pathological basis for both hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), although the predominant organ involvement and clinical severity differ between these syndromes. HFRS is mainly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Its clinical course is traditionally described in febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, diuretic, and convalescent phases, although these phases may overlap and are not uniformly observed in every patient [19]. The febrile phase typically presents with acute fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally visual disturbances. Progression to the hypotensive phase reflects increasing vascular permeability and may result in plasma leakage, hypotension, tachycardia, and circulatory shock. The subsequent oliguric phase is characterized by acute kidney injury, reduced urine output, proteinuria, hematuria, azotemia, and electrolyte disturbances. Recovery of renal function is followed by a diuretic phase, during which marked polyuria may produce significant fluid and electrolyte losses. The convalescent phase is charac- terized by gradual recovery, although fatigue and reduced physical capacity may persist for weeks or longer. Importantly, the clinical spectrum of HFRS is broad, ranging from the relatively mild nephropathia epidemica associated with Puumala virus to severe disease caused by Hantaan and Dobrava-Belgrade viruses [20]. This variation indicates that clinical outcome is influenced not only by the presence of hantavirus infection but also by virus-specific and host-related factors. HCPS is predominantly associated with New World hantaviruses, particularly Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. analysis.background: Emerging infectious diseases, driven by ecological and socioeconomic changes, have highlighted hantavirus as a globally important zoonosis with diverse clinical outcomes.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers reservoir ecology, disease spectrum (HFRS vs HCPS), endothelial‑mediated pathogenesis, diagnostic advances (ELISA, RT‑qPCR, RT‑LAMP, digital PCR, NGS, CRISPR), supportive and investigational therapies, vaccine platforms, and One Health surveillance.
analysis.current_state: Consensus exists on the zoonotic reservoir–virus associations, the spectrum of severe disease, the central role of supportive care, and the limited but promising antiviral and vaccine research.
analysis.gaps: Key uncertainties remain in early, affordable diagnostics, clinical validation of novel assays, cost and infrastructure barriers, limited antiviral options, and the lack of broadly protective vaccines.
analysis.future_research: Priorities include scalable genomic surveillance, validation of CRISPR‑based diagnostics, early risk‑prediction models, host‑directed therapeutics, and development of multivalent vaccines within a One Health framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Emerging infectious diseases, driven by ecological and socioeconomic changes, have highlighted hantavirus as a globally important zoonosis with diverse clinical outcomes. Main directions: The review covers reservoir ecology, disease spectrum (HFRS vs HCPS), endothelial‑mediated pathogenesis, diagnostic advances (ELISA, RT‑qPCR, RT‑LAMP, digital PCR, NGS, CRISPR), supportive and investigational therapies, vaccine platforms, and One Health surveillance. Current state: Consensus exists on the zoonotic reservoir–virus associations, the spectrum of severe disease, the central role of supportive care, and the limited but promising antiviral and vaccine research. Gaps: Key uncertainties remain in early, affordable diagnostics, clinical validation of novel assays, cost and infrastructure barriers, limited antiviral options, and the lack of broadly protective vaccines. Future research: Priorities include scalable genomic surveillance, validation of CRISPR‑based diagnostics, early risk‑prediction models, host‑directed therapeutics, and development of multivalent vaccines within a One Health framework.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 感染:流行病学、发病机制、诊断与预防的综合综述

analysis_zh.background: 新发传染病受生态和社会经济变化驱动,已凸显 汉坦病毒 为一种全球重要的动物源性疾病,临床表现多样。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述涵盖宿主动物生态、疾病谱(肾综合征出血热 vs 汉坦病毒肺综合征)、内皮介导的发病机制、诊断进展(ELISA、RT‐qPCR、RT‐LAMP、数字PCR、NGS、CRISPR)、支持治疗与研究性疗法、疫苗平台以及 One Health 监测。
analysis_zh.current_state: 在动物源性宿主‐病毒关联、重症疾病谱、支持治疗的核心作用以及有限但有前景的抗病毒和疫苗研究方面已达成共识。
analysis_zh.gaps: 关键不确定性仍包括早期、经济的诊断手段、创新检测的临床验证、成本与基础设施障碍、有限的抗病毒药物选择,以及缺乏广谱保护性疫苗。
analysis_zh.future_research: 优先事项包括可扩展的基因组监测、CRISPR 基础诊断的验证、早期风险预测模型、宿主靶向治疗,以及在 One Health 框架下开发多价疫苗。

papers.title: Hantavirus Infections: Virology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Spectrum, and Emerging Therapeutic Frontiers
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas. Despite advances in hantavirus biology and clinical management, no universally approved antiviral therapy exists, and severe HPS remains associated with high mortality. This review summarizes the current understanding of hantavirus virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, with emphasis on emerging therapeutic strategies. Hantavirus disease is characterized by profound vascular permeability despite limited direct cytopathic injury. Increasing evidence implicates immune-mediated endothelial dysfunction involving β3 integrins, CD8+ T-cell responses, angiopoietin/Tie2 dysregulation, vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, and neutrophil extracellular traps, thereby providing potential targets for antiviral and host-directed therapies. Clinical management remains predominantly supportive. Intravenous ribavirin may benefit patients when administered early in HFRS but has not demonstrated efficacy in established HPS. Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) has emerged as an important rescue therapy for severe HPS with cardiopulmonary collapse. Experimental approaches include favipiravir, direct-acting antivirals, convalescent plasma, broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, viral entry and fusion inhibitors, and strategies targeting pathological host responses. Next-generation vaccine platforms, including DNA vaccines, virus-like particle, and structure-guided subunit vaccines, are under investigation. Integrating structural virology, antiviral discovery, immunology, genomic surveillance, and One Health approaches will be essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the Americas.
analysis.main_directions: Emerging therapeutic strategies focus on immune‑mediated endothelial dysfunction (β3 integrins, CD8⁺ T‑cells, angiopoietin/Tie2, VEGF, NETs) and include antivirals, monoclonal antibodies, and host‑directed interventions.
analysis.current_state: Disease is characterized by profound vascular permeability despite limited direct cytopathic injury, and clinical management remains predominantly supportive.
analysis.gaps: No universally approved antiviral therapy exists and severe HPS continues to have high mortality despite recent advances.
analysis.future_research: Integrating structural virology, antiviral discovery, immunology, genomic surveillance, and One Health approaches will be essential for developing effective therapeutics and next‑generation vaccines.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HPS in the Americas. Main directions: Emerging therapies target immune‑mediated endothelial dysfunction (β3 integrins, CD8⁺ T‑cells, angiopoietin/Tie2, VEGF, NETs) and include antivirals, monoclonal antibodies, and host‑directed agents. Current state: Disease shows profound vascular permeability with limited cytopathic injury; care is mainly supportive. Gaps: No universally approved antiviral and severe HPS retains high mortality. Future research: Combine structural virology, antiviral discovery, immunology, genomic surveillance, and One Health to create effective treatments and vaccines.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 感染:病毒学、发病机制、临床范围及新兴治疗前沿

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致在欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热,以及在美洲的汉坦病毒肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 新兴治疗策略聚焦于免疫介导的内皮功能障碍(β3 整合素、CD8+ T细胞、血管生成素/Tie2、VEGF、NETs),并包括抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体以及宿主靶向干预。
analysis_zh.current_state: 该疾病特征为显著的血管通透性增加,尽管直接细胞毒性损伤有限,临床管理仍主要为支持性治疗。
analysis_zh.gaps: 尚无全球统一批准的抗病毒疗法,且尽管近期取得进展,重症HPS仍具有高死亡率。
analysis_zh.future_research: 整合结构病毒学、抗病毒药物发现、免疫学、基因组监测以及One Health方法,对于开发有效疗法和下一代疫苗至关重要。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致在欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热,以及在美洲的汉坦病毒肺综合征。 主要方向：新兴治疗策略聚焦于免疫介导的内皮功能障碍(β3 整合素、CD8+ T细胞、血管生成素/Tie2、VEGF、NETs),并包括抗病毒药物、单克隆… 研究现状：该疾病特征为显著的血管通透性增加,尽管直接细胞毒性损伤有限,临床管理仍主要为支持性治疗。 不足：尚无全球统一批准的抗病毒疗法,且尽管近期取得进展,重症HPS仍具有高死亡率。 后续研究：整合结构病毒学、抗病毒药物发现、免疫学、基因组监测以及One Health方法,对于开发有效疗法和下一代疫苗至关重要。

papers.title: Immunoinformatics based design and evaluation of a multi-epitope vaccine candidate targeting the envelopment polyprotein of Andes orthohantavirus.
papers.abstract: Andes Orthohantavirus is known to be the etiological agent for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which is a highly dangerous disease with a very high death rate. There is no vaccine available to date to protect against this disease. This project aimed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine for Andes Orthohantavirus using immunoinformatics. Epitopes of CTL, HTL, and B cell types were predicted for the shortlisted Glycoprotein precursor after testing antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and subcellular location. The chosen epitopes were combined using appropriate linkers and β-defensin as an adjuvant to create a multi-epitope vaccine. The final vaccine construct had a length of 296 amino acids and showed excellent antigenicity (0.7297), non-allergenicity, structural stability, and solubility properties. The structure of the vaccine construct showed that 94.6% of residues lie in the preferred areas of the Ramachandran plot, thus ensuring good stereochemistry. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis results confirmed the stable binding of the vaccine construct to TLR-3 receptors. At the same time, immune simulation revealed a fast degradation of antigens, production of antibodies, memory B-cells, and cytokines. In silico cloning integrated the codon-optimized gene with a CAI value of 0.97 and a GC percentage of 49.77% into the plasmid vector pET-28a(+). The designed multi-epitope vaccine displayed good predicted immunogenicity, structure, and expression properties that made it suitable to be used as a potential vaccine candidate against Andes Orthohantavirus infection. Further experimental validation is needed to assess its safety and effectiveness.

analysis.background: Andes Orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, a highly dangerous disease with a very high death rate, and no vaccine is currently available.
analysis.methods: The study used immunoinformatics to predict CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor, screened them for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity and subcellular location, linked the selected epitopes with β‑defensin adjuvant, and evaluated the construct by structural modeling, Ramachandran analysis, molecular docking to TLR‑3, normal mode analysis, immune simulation, and in‑silico cloning.
analysis.results: The 296‑aa vaccine showed an antigenicity score of 0.7297, was non‑allergenic, 94.6 % of residues fell in favored Ramachandran regions, docked stably to TLR‑3, induced simulated antibody and cytokine responses, and the codon‑optimized gene achieved a CAI of 0.97 with 49.77 % GC in the pET‑28a(+) vector.
analysis.contribution: The work presents a computationally validated multi‑epitope vaccine candidate that could be pursued as a potential prophylactic against Andes Orthohantavirus infection.
analysis.limitations: Results are derived solely from in‑silico analyses presented in the abstract; experimental validation of safety and efficacy is still needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes Orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with high mortality and no vaccine exists. Methods: Immunoinformatics predicted CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor, filtered them, linked with β‑defensin, and assessed the construct via structural modeling, Ramachandran analysis, docking to TLR‑3, normal mode analysis, immune simulation, and in‑silico cloning. Results: The 296‑aa vaccine scored 0.7297 antigenicity, was non‑allergenic, 94.6% residues in favored Ramachandran regions, docked stably to TLR‑3, elicited simulated antibody and cytokine responses, and the codon‑optimized gene had CAI 0.97 and 49.77% GC in pET‑28a(+). Contribution: It provides a computationally validated multi‑epitope vaccine candidate for Andes Orthohantavirus. Limitations: Findings are based only on abstract‑level in‑silico data; experimental validation is required.

papers.title: Hantaviruses Through the Lens of Intrinsic Disorder: Structural Plasticity, Pathogenesis, and Therapeutic Opportunities
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens responsible for two major clinical syndromes, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Despite encoding only a limited repertoire of structural proteins, hantaviruses efficiently manipulate host cellular machinery through highly multifunctional viral proteins. Increasing evidence indicates that intrinsic protein disorder plays a central role in enabling this functional versatility. This review integrates current knowledge on hantavirus epidemiology, transmission dynamics, genome organization, pathophysiology, and therapeutic development while highlighting the emerging importance of intrinsically disordered protein regions in viral biology. Bioinformatic analyses demonstrate that all major hantavirus proteins, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L), envelope glycoprotein precursor (Gn/Gc), and nucleocapsid protein (N) contain flexible or intrinsically disordered regions that facilitate diverse molecular interactions. These structurally dynamic regions contribute to viral RNA encapsulation, replication, receptor recognition, membrane fusion, immune evasion, virion assembly, and modulation of host antiviral responses. The remarkable structural plasticity of hantavirus proteins provides a mechanistic explanation for their multifunctionality and distinct pathogenic manifestations observed between Old World and New World hantaviruses. Furthermore, intrinsic disorder represents a promising yet underexplored avenue for antiviral intervention, complementing current approaches based on antivirals, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, and host-directed therapies. Advances in artificial intelligence-driven structural prediction and disorder analysis are rapidly expanding our understanding of these dynamic proteins and may accelerate the identification of novel therapeutic targets. Collectively, this review emphasizes that intrinsic disorder is not merely a structural characteristic of hantavirus proteins but a fundamental determinant of viral adaptability, pathogenicity, and evolutionary success, offering new perspectives for future mechanistic studies and rational antiviral design.

Despite encoding only a limited repertoire of structural proteins, hantaviruses efficiently manipulate host cellular machinery through highly multifunctional viral proteins. Increasing evidence indicates that intrinsic protein disorder plays a central role in enabling this functional versatility. This review integrates current knowledge on hantavirus epidemiology, transmission dynamics, genome organization, pathophysiology, and therapeutic development while highlighting the emerging importance of intrinsically disordered protein regions in viral biology. Bioinformatic analyses demonstrate that all major hantavirus proteins, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L), envelope glycoprotein precursor (Gn/Gc), and nucleocapsid protein (N) contain flexible or intrinsically disordered regions that facilitate diverse molecular interactions. These structurally dynamic regions contribute to viral RNA encapsulation, replication, receptor recognition, membrane fusion, immune evasion, virion assembly, and modulation of host antiviral responses. The remarkable structural plasticity of hantavirus proteins provides a mechanistic explanation for their multifunctionality and distinct pathogenic manifestations observed between Old World and New World hantaviruses. Furthermore, intrinsic disorder represents a promising yet underexplored avenue for antiviral intervention, complementing current approaches based on antivirals, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, and host-directed therapies. Advances in artificial intelligence-driven structural prediction and disorder analysis are rapidly expanding our understanding of these dynamic proteins and may accelerate the identification of novel therapeutic targets. Collectively, this review emphasizes that intrinsic disorder is not merely a structural characteristic of hantavirus proteins but a fundamental determinant of viral adaptability, pathogenicity, and evolutionary success, offering new perspectives for future mechanistic studies and rational antiviral design.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, both with high morbidity and mortality (A1).
analysis.methods: Methods are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: Intrinsic protein disorder is present in all major hantavirus proteins (L, Gn/Gc, N) and underlies their multifunctionality, affecting RNA encapsulation, replication, receptor binding, membrane fusion, immune evasion, assembly, and host response modulation (A5, A6). analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒在全球分布,是人畜共患的病原体,可导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,两者均具有高发病率和高死亡率 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 所提供的证据中未报告方法。
analysis_zh.results: 内在蛋白质无序性存在于所有主要的汉坦病毒蛋白(L、Gn/Gc、N)中,并构成其多功能性的基础,影响RNA包装、复制、受体结合、膜融合、免疫逃逸、组装以及宿主反应调节 (A5, A6)。这种无序性可能解释旧世界与新世界汉坦病毒之间的致病差异 (A7),并被强调为抗病毒策略的有前景靶点 (A8)。基于人工智能的结构预测正在拓展对这些无序区域的认识 (A9)。

analysis_zh.limitations: 该文章仅为综述摘要;未提供原始数据、详细方法或定量结果 (abstract_only)。

papers.title: Hantavirus at the Climate-Rodent-Human Interface: Integrating Immunopathogenesis, Ecological Drivers, and Health Inequities in the Americas.
papers.abstract: New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) within heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings across the Americas. This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement.
