This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement. 1. Introduction New World orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a rapidly progressive illness characterized by capillary leak, pulmonary edema, shock, and, in severe cases, cardiorespiratory failure. The syndrome was recognized internationally after the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States, and subsequent surveillance established a heterogeneous distribution of pathogenic orthohantaviruses across North, Central, and South America. Although HCPS is uncommon compared with many endemic infections, case fatality remains substantial and varies by virus, setting, clinical recognition, and access to supportive care. The major New World viruses illustrate why a single continental model is inadequate. Sin Nombre virus (SNV) predominates among recognized cases in the United States, Andes virus (ANDV) is a major cause of HCPS in Argentina and Chile and can be transmitted from person to person, and Choclo virus (CHOV) sustains endemic transmission in Panama. South America also contains extensive viral and reservoir diversity, including Juquitiba- and Araraquara-associated transmission systems in Brazil. This diversity affects reservoir ecology, transmission opportunities, immune interactions, and the design of surveillance systems. Hantavirus risk is usually described through the climate–rodent–human interface. Climatic variability and landscape change influence vegetation and food availability, which can alter reservoir abundance and movement; housing, occupation, and human behavior then shape whether infected rodents and people share the same spaces. That ecological pathway is necessary but incomplete. Exposure does not invariably produce infection, and infection does not invariably progress to severe HCPS. The transition from infection to clinical disease depends on viral entry, innate sensing and immune evasion, endothelial barrier regulation, cellular immune responses, and humoral immunity. The final transition, from clinically apparent infection to a documented outcome, also depends on case ascertainment and care pathways. Early HCPS symptoms are nonspecific, confirmatory assays and referral services vary across settings, and severe disease may require specialized critical care. These conditions plausibly affect recognition and management, although available comparative studies do not quantify their independent contribution to differences in case fatality. Serosurveys from particular Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous geographic and exposure contexts; they do not support assumptions of ethnicity-based intrinsic biological susceptibility. This review examines how ecological exposure, host immune responses, and structural conditions may be connected along a mechanism-to-population continuum, with emphasis on settings for which primary human and reservoir evidence is available. Its purpose is to identify supported links and explicitly distinguish them from cross-level hypotheses that require prospective testing. 2. Methodology We conducted a critical narrative review integrating clinical, epidemiological, ecological, and mechanistic evidence on New World orthohantaviruses in the Americas within a One Health framework. The literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos, and LILACS, from database inception through 29 September 2026, without language restrictions. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH/DeCS), where applicable, and free-text terms adapted to each database, covering hantaviruses and relevant New World viruses, reservoir ecology, climate, land use, transmission, immunopathogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, clinical management, surveillance, and structural determinants of health (Supplementary Tables S1–S4). The PubMed/MEDLINE search was updated on 27 October 2026. Additional relevant publications were identified through reference-list screening. Institutional public-health reports and peer-reviewed surveillance studies were selected based on source credibility, geographic relevance, temporal coverage, and traceability to provide complementary context on regional epidemiological patterns, surveillance activities, and public-health responses. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts, and potentially relevant full texts, resolving disagreements through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Publications were selected based on relevance, directness of evidence, and contextual applicability. Priority was given to clinical and epidemiological investigations, reservoir and environmental studies, and experimental research with mechanistic relevance. Relevant reviews and reports from recognized national or regional public-health institutions were also considered. Publications with limited thematic relevance, insufficiently supported findings, or unclear geographic or ecological applicability were not prioritized. Seventy-six sources are cited in this review. Relevant information was extracted on study design, geographic setting, viral species, study population or ecological context, principal findings, and methodological limitations. Evidence was organized and synthesized thematically, considering consistency across studies, directness of findings, and inferential limitations. Experimental evidence, observational associations, and proposed mechanistic or population-level relationships were distinguished during interpretation. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or certainty-of-evidence grading was performed for individual studies. The Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) informed the scientific reasoning, referencing, and presentation of the review (Supplementary Table S8). Figures were prepared using BioRender, including its integrated generative artificial intelligence tools. 3. Viral Diversity and Reservoir Ecology Across the Americas Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with segmented genomes. In the Americas, clinically important lineages are maintained primarily in sigmodontine and neotomine rodents, although viral RNA or antibodies have been detected in additional small-mammal species. Detection in a species is not sufficient to establish reservoir competence; a competent reservoir must sustain infection and contribute to onward viral maintenance and shedding. In North America, SNV is the dominant recognized cause of HCPS in the United States and is strongly associated with the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. Surveillance identifies heterogeneity in location and genotype, but reports from the United States should not be extrapolated uncritically to Canada or Mexico. A 2019 review of Mexico found multiple rodent-associated hantaviruses but no confirmed human hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the publications assessed at that time. Canada, by contrast, has a documented national experience: 143 laboratory-confirmed SNV-associated HCPS cases had been reported up to 1 January 2020, together with a reviewed account of local ecology, biology, and viral genetics. Caribbean evidence is sparser but not absent; in Barbados, retrospective and prospective testing of patients with febrile illness detected orthohantavirus-specific antibodies between 2008 and 2016, with higher prevalence during the rainy season and among urban residents. For much of the remaining Caribbean and for large parts of Mexico, the evidence assembled here is too sparse for a comparable synthesis of human burden, virus diversity, or reservoir dynamics; an absence of studies should not be interpreted as absence of circulation. Panama is among the best-characterized Central American systems. Surveillance during 1999–2019 defined an endemic area encompassing approximately 27% of Panama’s national territory, not 27% of districts or cases; this mapped area does not exclude circulation elsewhere. Choclo virus (CHOV) is associated with the reservoir Oligoryzomys costaricensis, the Costa Rican pygmy rice rat; earlier Panamanian reports assigned this host to Oligoryzomys fulvescens, which accounts for the divergence between earlier and current nomenclature rather than indicating two distinct reservoirs. Systematic rodent sampling at more than 150 sites across Panama has since characterized this host, with overall hantavirus seroprevalence above 15% in the pygmy rice rat and seropositive animals concentrated in central-western Panama, where human CHOV incidence is also highest. Recognition of both HCPS and hantavirus fever increased following the introduction of decentralized testing and standardized surveillance, although such programmatic observations do not isolate the effects of individual health-system changes. South America contains multiple virus–host systems, including ANDV in the southern Andes, Juquitiba virus associated with Oligoryzomys nigripes, and Araraquara virus associated with Necromys lasiurus in Brazil. The recognized range extends to the Guiana Shield, where Maripa virus has been confirmed as a cause of HCPS in a documented case series from French Guiana. Reports from Bolivia, Peru, and northern Argentina continue to extend both the geographic range and the inventory of implicated viruses, including HCPS in Santa Cruz and Tarija, Rio Mamoré virus endemicity in the Peruvian Amazon, and a newly described orthohantavirus associated with HCPS in northern Argentina; a narrative synthesis of rodent hosts and genotypes in southern South America describes the corresponding host–virus associations. Host composition, landscape structure, and longitudinal reservoir dynamics may affect local spillover probability, but these relationships cannot be translated into uniform continental incidence estimates. Epidemiologic and genomic investigations document limited person-to-person ANDV transmission in some close-contact settings. Human and reservoir data remain much less complete for several countries and for culturally distinct communities within countries. Reservoir infection is commonly persistent and clinically inapparent, allowing viral maintenance without obvious disease in the host population. Demography, movement, aggressive encounters, and density can alter transmission within reservoir populations, while local extinction and reintroduction can produce temporally unstable foci. These features mean that a single cross-sectional rodent survey provides only a snapshot of a dynamic system. The regional inventory in Supplementary Table S5 makes this asymmetry explicit: evidence is comparatively rich for SNV in the United States, CHOV in Panama, ANDV in Chile and Argentina, and several Brazilian systems, but is less detailed for much of Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean, and several countries in northern South America. These categories describe the sources used in this review, not verified absence of infection elsewhere. 4. Environmental and Socioecological Pathways of Exposure Climate affects hantavirus risk indirectly through ecological processes rather than through a uniform, linear relationship with human incidence. In arid and semi-arid systems, increased precipitation can increase primary productivity and food availability, followed by growth in reservoir populations and greater opportunities for human contact. Across Latin America and the Caribbean, however, the direction and magnitude of associations with precipitation and temperature vary among settings, reflecting differences in reservoir species, seasonality, land use, and human behavior. In northwestern Argentina, synchronous increases in rodent abundance have preceded HCPS activity, consistent with the value of longitudinal ecological monitoring while also illustrating the need for local calibration. Land-use change can modify both reservoir communities and human exposure. Forest fragmentation, agricultural expansion, and habitat conversion may favor generalist rodents in some landscapes and increase the frequency with which people work or live near reservoir habitat. Studies from Brazil have linked landscape configuration, sugarcane expansion, climate, and social variables with modeled or observed hantavirus risk, but the effects are context-dependent and should not be generalized as universal consequences of deforestation or warming. A systematic review of land-cover and land-use exposures likewise reported heterogeneous, setting-specific associations with human hantavirus infection risk rather than a consistent directional effect. At the point of contact, occupation and housing shape whether ecological hazard becomes individual exposure. Agricultural and forestry work, entry into poorly ventilated structures, sweeping or cleaning rodent-contaminated spaces, grain handling, and peridomestic rodent activity can increase contact with infectious urine, feces, or saliva. A systematic review found measurable hantavirus seroprevalence among agricultural and forestry workers, while case investigations in the United States have repeatedly identified household and occupational settings as plausible exposure sites. Exposure prevention is therefore not reducible to knowledge alone. In an endemic community in Panama, preventive practices were associated with perceived barriers, education, and community experience of disease; the authors argued for community-based interventions that address practical obstacles rather than relying exclusively on information campaigns. These findings are important for equity: recommendations that require structural housing repairs, specialized protective equipment, or changes in livelihood may be biologically reasonable but difficult to implement without material support. Across disciplines, the inference is uneven. Longitudinal ecological observations and geographically explicit modeling can associate reservoir dynamics with environmental conditions, but usually do not measure the infectious dose received by individual people. Occupational investigations more directly identify contact opportunities; however, links from such exposure to early immune control or eventual mortality remain rarely measured within the same population. Accordingly, each proposed transition should be tested rather than treated as a proven causal chain (Supplementary Table S6). Figure 1 depicts an explicitly hypothesized pathway from ecological change to recognized clinical outcomes; Supplementary Table S6 identifies the type of evidence and measurable indicator for each proposed link. The climatic and landscape associations are setting-specific, while diagnostic delay and critical-care capacity are proposed modifiers that have not been shown to explain regional mortality differences independently. 5. From Exposure to Infection: Viral Entry and Early Host Response Human infection most often follows inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with rodent excreta, although direct contact with contaminated material and, less commonly, bites can also provide routes of exposure. ANDV adds a distinct pathway because close-contact person-to-person transmission is documented, including household and nosocomial clusters. The existence of these routes does not imply that every exposure produces infection: inhaled dose, environmental stability, route of entry, viral genotype, and host factors all influence whether productive infection is established. Protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been identified experimentally as an essential entry factor for ANDV and SNV in the tested cellular and animal systems. This result supports a specific virus–host interaction; it does not establish a PCDH1 requirement for every New World orthohantavirus or explain interindividual variation in clinical severity. The relative importance of entry co-factors and tissue-specific susceptibility remains unresolved. Vascular endothelial cells are central to HCPS pathology, but infection is largely non-cytolytic. Endothelial infection therefore differs from diseases in which extensive direct cell destruction explains organ failure. papers.full_text: Hantavirus receptor recognition: From structural insights to therapeutic opportunities Hantavirus infections illustrate a persistent gap between advances in molecular virology and the availability of targeted clinical interventions. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV), cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which can progress rapidly to respiratory failure and shock. Old World hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), often involving acute kidney injury and vascular dysfunction. No vaccine is licensed for HCPS, and no targeted antiviral treatment has established efficacy for hantavirus syndromes. Inactivated HFRS vaccines are used in parts of Asia, although their performance varies across settings. Early recognition and skilled supportive care therefore remain central to patient outcomes. Preventing infection before a virus enters its target cells offers an attractive therapeutic opportunity. For many viruses, protective antibodies work by blocking attachment or membrane fusion. In 2018, we identified protocadherin‐1 (PCDH1) as a critical entry receptor for ANDV and SNV, including in human endothelial cells, which are major targets of hantavirus infection. Subsequent studies showed that direct engagement of PCDH1 is important for ANDV pathogenesis in a Syrian hamster model. Yet a fundamental question remained: how does the assembled hantavirus spike recognize this receptor? Our recent study in Nature resolves this interaction at near‐atomic resolution. Rather than binding an individual glycoprotein subunit, a single PCDH1 molecule engages a deep central cavity formed by four Gn subunits of the Gn–Gc spike. Complementary structural, functional, and large‐scale mutational analyses identified regions of Gn critical for receptor recognition. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for developing strategies to prevent hantavirus entry (Table 1). Translational opportunities arising from the structural and functional characterization of hantavirus receptor recognition. Area Key findings and implications Priorities for translation Therapeutic antibodies Neutralizing antibodies block receptor engagement through distinct mechanisms, supporting the development of antibodies with complementary activities. Evaluate neutralization breadth, resistance, and therapeutic efficacy after infection. Entry inhibitors Defining the PCDH1‐binding interface provides opportunities to develop engineered binding proteins, receptor mimetics, and small‐molecule inhibitors Identify and evaluate candidates for antiviral potency, specificity, and safety. Vaccine development Structural insights into Gn–Gc organization in the context of receptor binding and antibody recognition could inform the design of immunogens that elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies Assess the breadth, durability, and protective efficacy of vaccine‐induced responses. Antiviral resistance Functional mapping of receptor‐binding determinants can identify regions of the viral spike that are less tolerant of mutations Define potential escape pathways and their effects on viral entry and fitness Broad‐spectrum countermeasures The possibility of analogous receptor‐binding sites in divergent hantaviruses raises opportunities for identifying shared therapeutic targets Establish receptor usage in Old World hantaviruses and assess conservation of the binding surface One immediate implication concerns therapeutic antibodies. A recessed receptor‐binding pocket might seem largely inaccessible to conventional antibodies. Nevertheless, our work explains how different potent neutralizing antibodies interfere with PCDH1 engagement. ANDV‐5 and MIB22 bind near the opening of the central cavity and directly block access to the PCDH1‐binding site, whereas ADI‐65534 and ANDV‐34 bind more peripheral epitopes and prevent receptor engagement through steric interference mediated by their antibody constant regions. Thus, an antibody need not bind the deepest part of a receptor pocket to block an essential entry event. This distinction provides a rationale for evaluating antibodies that recognize accessible, non‐overlapping surfaces and for considering combinations with complementary mechanisms. The therapeutic potential of neutralizing antibodies is supported by studies demonstrating post‐exposure protection against lethal ANDV infection in Syrian hamsters, using an MIB22‐containing antibody cocktail and the engineered broadly neutralizing antibody ADI‐65534, although clinical efficacy remains unproven. A second opportunity is to develop agents that interrupt the virus‐receptor interface without using conventional antibodies. Smaller antibody formats, including single‐domain antibodies, could potentially approach recessed surfaces that are difficult for larger molecules to access. Soluble receptor mimetics or other engineered binding proteins offer additional conceptual routes to prevent attachment. The structure also supplies a starting point for evaluating whether the pocket or its surrounding surfaces can be targeted by small molecules. These approaches will require further investigation to determine whether they can safely and effectively block viral infection. Spike‐directed agents may also have advantages over broadly disrupting PCDH1 itself, which has normal functions in host tissues. Beyond blocking receptor engagement, understanding the architecture of the hantavirus spike could also guide the development of more effective countermeasures. For several important human viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, stabilizing viral surface proteins in their prefusion state has been instrumental in developing vaccines that elicit potent neutralizing antibodies. Encouragingly, a recent study demonstrated that a prefusion‐stabilized Hantaan virus glycoprotein vaccine enhanced neutralizing antibody responses and reduced viral burdens in mice. Our findings could inform similar vaccine‐design strategies against HCPS‐causing viruses. Moreover, identifying ways to prevent the structural changes required for viral entry could reveal additional targets for antiviral development. Two important uncertainties remain. First, even conserved entry interfaces may tolerate changes that reduce inhibitor binding while retaining sufficient viral function. The development of scalable entry systems and deep mutational profiling approaches, as demonstrated in our study, provides an opportunity to systematically define the functional constraints governing receptor recognition. Extending such approaches to antibody escape, entry competence, and fusion could help identify vulnerable regions of the spike, anticipate resistance pathways, and guide the selection of therapeutic targets. Second, PCDH1 is not an established receptor for the Old World hantaviruses responsible for HFRS. Nevertheless, the corresponding central cavity of their glycoprotein spikes might serve as a binding site for unidentified receptors. If confirmed, this could reveal a shared vulnerability across divergent hantaviruses and provide opportunities for developing broadly acting therapeutics against both HCPS‐ and HFRS‐causing viruses. Promising candidates will need to demonstrate activity against phylogenetically distinct viruses, an acceptable safety profile, and benefit in appropriate preclinical models, including when treatment begins after infection. An important clinical question is whether blocking entry remains beneficial after symptom onset, when host inflammatory responses and vascular injury may already be established. The limited availability of animal models that reproduce human disease and the specialized containment required for studies with pathogenic hantaviruses remain significant practical obstacles. Our findings provide a structural and functional framework for developing new antibody‐based therapeutics, entry inhibitors, and improved vaccine strategies against pathogenic hantaviruses. analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause severe diseases such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and have high mortality; no licensed vaccine exists for HCPS and antiviral options are limited, revealing a gap between molecular virology advances and clinical interventions.
analysis.methods: The authors used near‑atomic cryo‑EM to resolve the hantavirus Gn‑Gc spike bound to the entry receptor protocadherin‑1, and complemented this with functional assays and large‑scale mutational analyses to map receptor‑binding determinants.
analysis.results: A single PCDH1 molecule engages a deep central cavity formed by four Gn subunits; critical Gn regions for receptor recognition were identified; neutralizing antibodies block this interaction by direct or steric mechanisms, and antibody cocktails protected Syrian hamsters from lethal ANDV infection, though clinical efficacy is unproven.
analysis.contribution: The structural and functional insights provide a molecular framework for developing entry inhibitors, therapeutic antibodies, engineered binding proteins, and prefusion‑stabilized vaccine immunogens, advancing translational strategies against hantaviruses.
analysis.limitations: Protective effects of antibodies are demonstrated only in animal models, and clinical efficacy remains unproven.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause severe HCPS and HFRS with high mortality and lack licensed vaccines or proven antivirals, highlighting a gap between molecular knowledge and therapies. Methods: Near‑atomic cryo‑EM of the Gn‑Gc spike bound to protocadherin‑1, plus functional and mutational analyses, defined receptor‑binding sites. Results: PCDH1 inserts into a cavity formed by four Gn subunits; key Gn residues were mapped; neutralizing antibodies block entry by steric or direct obstruction, and antibody cocktails protected hamsters, though clinical efficacy is unproven. Contribution: These data offer a framework for entry inhibitors, therapeutic antibodies, engineered proteins, and prefusion‑stabilized vaccines. Limitations: Efficacy shown only in animal models; clinical benefit remains unproven.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 受体识别:从结构洞察到治疗机会。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致严重疾病,如 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)和 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),且死亡率高;目前尚无 HCPS 的获批疫苗,抗病毒药物选择有限,暴露出分子病毒学进展与临床干预之间的鸿沟。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者采用近原子分辨率冷冻电镜解析了 汉坦病毒 Gn‐Gc 棘与入侵受体 protocadherin‐1 的复合结构,并结合功能实验和大规模突变分析绘制受体结合决定因素图谱。
analysis_zh.results: 单个 PCDH1 分子与由四个 Gn 亚基形成的深部中心腔结合;鉴定出 Gn 的关键区域负责受体识别;中和抗体通过直接或立体阻断机制抑制该相互作用,抗体鸡尾酒能够保护叙利亚仓鼠免受致死性 ANDV 感染,然而临床疗效尚未证实。
analysis_zh.contribution: 结构与功能洞察为开发入侵抑制剂、治疗性抗体、工程化结合蛋白和前融合稳定化疫苗免疫原提供了分子框架,推动针对 汉坦病毒es 的转化策略。
analysis_zh.limitations: 抗体的保护作用仅在动物模型中得到验证,临床疗效仍未证实。

papers.title: Ecological Correlates and Spatiotemporal Trends of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in West Kazakhstan: A 25-Year One Health Surveillance Study (2001-2025).
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis of public health concern in West Kazakhstan, yet long-term studies linking human and reservoir surveillance are scarce. We analyzed laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases (2001-2025) and routine rodent surveillance data from five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region within a One Health framework. Associations were estimated using negative binomial regression with district fixed effects and year-clustered robust standard errors (2002-2024; 115 district-years). Overall, 314 cases were recorded (81.2% male), with a major outbreak in 2005 (85 cases) and a resurgence in 2024-2025 (27 and 41 cases). Burlinsky District reported the most cases (44.9%), whereas Baiterek District had the highest incidence in 2016-2025. Of 132,694 rodents examined, 1083 (0.82%) were hantavirus antigen-positive. A larger share of the annual Mus musculus catch obtained in spring-summer was associated with higher case counts (incidence rate ratio 1.051 per percentage point; 95% CI: 1.024-1.080), and this was robust to excluding outbreak years. The number of positive rodents was associated with cases, but not after standardization for sampling effort. These associations do not establish M. musculus as a reservoir and are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, increased peridomestic exposure.

We analyzed laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases (2001-2025) and routine rodent surveillance data from five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region within a One Health framework. Associations were estimated using negative binomial regression with district fixed effects and year-clustered robust standard errors (2002-2024; 115 district-years). Overall, 314 cases were recorded (81.2% male), with a major outbreak in 2005 (85 cases) and a resurgence in 2024-2025 (27 and 41 cases). Burlinsky District reported the most cases (44.9%), whereas Baiterek District had the highest incidence in 2016-2025. Of 132,694 rodents examined, 1083 (0.82%) were hantavirus antigen-positive. A larger share of the annual Mus musculus catch obtained in spring-summer was associated with higher case counts (incidence rate ratio 1.051 per percentage point; 95% CI: 1.024-1.080), and this was robust to excluding outbreak years. The number of positive rodents was associated with cases, but not after standardization for sampling effort. These associations do not establish M. musculus as a reservoir and are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, increased peridomestic exposure.

Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis caused by orthohantaviruses. It is characterized by acute fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and renal dysfunction, and causes substantial morbidity and mortality across Eurasia. Although China reports most of the global HFRS burden, the disease remains an important problem in neighboring countries, including Russia and Kazakhstan. In West Kazakhstan, particularly in areas bordering the Russian Federation, HFRS persists as a public health concern because rural and peri-urban populations live in close proximity to natural foci of infection. The West Kazakhstan Region is the only officially recognized HFRS-endemic region of Kazakhstan with registered human cases. The first case was detected in 2000, and natural foci of orthohantaviruses have been described in its northern districts. HFRS transmission is shaped by interacting ecological factors, including reservoir population density, environmental conditions, and anthropogenic land-use change. Rodent species occupy distinct niches, including woodland, open steppe, and peridomestic structures, and their distribution influences where and how often humans are exposed. Climate and humidity affect food availability for rodents and the environmental persistence of virus shed in excreta, which is the main source of human infection by inhalation. Agricultural expansion and landscape features that increase human–rodent contact further raise the probability of spillover. Most epidemiological studies of HFRS have focused on outbreak investigations or short-term trends. Voutilainen et al. showed that intensive forest management altered Puumala orthohantavirus infection in boreal bank vole populations, and Zhang et al. identified environmental and meteorological factors associated with HFRS incidence in Weifang, China. Long-term studies that analyze human and reservoir surveillance data jointly remain concentrated in China and Russia, and comparable evidence from other endemic regions, including Kazakhstan, is limited. Linking human epidemiological trends with reservoir ecology over long periods can help public health authorities assess risk in endemic areas. This study applied a One Health framework, integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance data. Our objectives were to describe the spatiotemporal distribution of HFRS in five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region over 2001–2025, and to quantify associations between human HFRS case counts and reservoir indicators (the seasonal distribution of rodent captures by species, rodent hantavirus positivity, and human seroprevalence), while accounting for time-invariant differences between districts. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design, Area, and Periods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal ecological study in five administrative units of the West Kazakhstan Region: Burlinsky, Baiterek, Chingirlau, and Terekty districts and Uralsk City (Table 1; Figure 1). Human case data are described for the full period 2001–2025. Inferential analyses were restricted to 2002–2024 (5 districts × 23 years = 115 district-years) because no spring–summer rodent trapping was performed in 2001 and spring–summer rodent data for 2025 were not yet available at the time of analysis. 2.2. Human Case Data and Case Definition Data on all HFRS cases registered from 2001 to 2025 were obtained from the Ural Anti-Plague Station. Each record included year, district of residence, and sex. A case was defined as a patient with a clinically compatible illness and laboratory confirmation according to the national clinical protocols in force at the time, most recently the Clinical Protocol for Diagnosis and Treatment of HFRS of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Kazakhstan (29 March 2019, Protocol No. 60), which defines serological confirmation as a fourfold or greater rise in antibody titer in paired sera collected 10–12 days apart. Laboratory confirmation was performed at the laboratory of the Ural Anti-Plague Station by detection of hantavirus-specific IgM antibodies and/or a fourfold or greater rise in IgG antibody titer by ELISA, using the “VectoHanta-IgM” and “VectoHanta-IgG” test systems (JSC Vector-Best, Novosibirsk, Russia). Molecular testing (RT-PCR) was not performed, so the infecting orthohantavirus species was not determined. Testing of patients for leptospirosis was not systematically recorded. District population estimates were obtained from the Bureau of National Statistics of the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2016–2025. District incidence was therefore calculated for 2016–2025 only. Regional incidence was calculated using the total population of the West Kazakhstan Region. Because the official 2025 regional estimate was not yet available, the 2025 regional incidence was estimated using the 2024 population. 2.3. Rodent Surveillance Rodent monitoring was conducted by the Ural Anti-Plague Station as part of routine zoonotic surveillance at 49–50 fixed sites in the study area, located in natural habitats (riparian forest, steppe, and fields) and within or adjacent to settlements. Surveys were conducted twice yearly, in spring–summer (May–August) and autumn–winter (October–January). Rodents were captured with Gero snap traps and live traps (box and mesh traps) baited with black bread soaked in unrefined sunflower oil, with approximately 500–1000 trap-nights per season. Exact trap-night totals were not available. Between 2001 and 2025, 132,694 rodents were examined (47,042 in spring–summer and 85,652 in autumn–winter; Table 2). Species were identified by trained zoologists on the basis of external morphology and cranial and dental characters using standard identification keys. Four species were analyzed: the bank vole (Myodes glareolus), the common vole (Microtus arvalis), the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), and the house mouse (Mus musculus). For each species and year, the seasonal distribution of captures was expressed as the percentage of that year’s captures of the species obtained in spring–summer. The autumn–winter value is its complement (100% minus the spring–summer value). This indicator describes the seasonal timing of captures within each species. It is not the species’ share of the rodent community and not a measure of absolute abundance. Rodents were tested for hantavirus antigen in lung tissue by ELISA using the “Hantagnost” test system (M.P. Chumakov Federal Scientific Center for Research and Development of Immunobiological Preparations of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Institute of Poliomyelitis, Moscow, Russia). Rodent positivity was recorded as the annual number of antigen-positive animals and, for sensitivity analysis, as the percentage of positive animals among all rodents examined in that year. Rodents, including M. musculus, were not typed for hantaviruses by RT-PCR or sequencing. Rodents were also tested for Leptospira by PCR using the “AmpliSens” assay (Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, Moscow, Russia). Rodent indicators were available only at the regional level. The same annual values were therefore assigned to all five districts. 2.4. Human Seroprevalence Human hantavirus seroprevalence (“population immunity”) was measured in serological surveys of adult residents of HFRS-risk areas, conducted by the laboratory of the Ural Anti-Plague Station over 10 years (2006, 2007, 2009, 2011–2014, 2016, 2024, and 2025). In each survey, 72–333 adult residents were tested for hantavirus-specific IgG antibodies by ELISA using the “VectoHanta-IgG” test system (JSC Vector-Best, Novosibirsk, Russia). In total, 1799 persons were tested. Seroprevalence was calculated as the percentage of IgG-positive persons among those tested. 2.5. Statistical Analysis Variables are summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD), median (range), or n (%). Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between district-level annual case counts and the rodent indicators (n = 115 district-years). Because human seroprevalence was available for only 10 years, its correlation with annual regional case counts was assessed at the year level. Because the outcome is an overdispersed count, the primary model was negative binomial (NB2) regression with a log link and district fixed effects (Baiterek District as the reference), with the seasonal distribution of M. musculus captures and the number of antigen-positive rodents as predictors. Other species were not retained because they showed no association in bivariate analysis. Overdispersion was assessed with the Pearson χ2/df of the corresponding Poisson model and a likelihood-ratio test of the NB dispersion parameter (α = 0). Because the rodent predictors vary only between years, standard errors were clustered by year (23 clusters). No population offset was used because district populations were not available before 2016. The district fixed effects absorb stable differences in population size between districts. Results are reported as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). To address the specification of the panel model, we also fitted a linear model and compared pooled ordinary least squares (OLS), random-effects (RE), and fixed-effects (FE) specifications. District heterogeneity was assessed with an F-test of district effects (FE vs. pooled OLS) and the Breusch–Pagan Lagrange multiplier test (RE vs. pooled OLS). A Hausman test (FE vs. RE) could not be meaningfully computed because the predictors take identical values for all districts in a given year. They therefore have no between-district variation, and the FE, RE, and pooled OLS slope estimates are identical. Serial correlation was assessed with the Wooldridge test, groupwise heteroskedasticity with the modified Wald test, and multicollinearity with variance inflation factors (VIFs). These diagnostics were used to justify the choice of the count model as the primary analysis. Four sensitivity analyses were conducted. The primary model was refitted after excluding 2024, the year with the most extreme spring–summer M. musculus value, and after excluding the 2005 outbreak year. It was also refitted with the percentage of positive rodents among those examined in place of the number of positive rodents, to account for sampling effort, and at the regional year level (n = 23). Analyses were performed in Stata version 16 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). A p-value < 0.05 was considered significant. A generative artificial intelligence tool (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA) was used to assist with the re-analysis of the surveillance data, including writing analysis code, computing preliminary estimates, and preparing Figure 2 and Figure 3. All estimates reported in this manuscript were reproduced independently by the authors in Stata, and the authors verified all figures against the source data. 2.6. Ethical Considerations The study used anonymized, aggregated surveillance data. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of West Kazakhstan Marat Ospanov Medical University (approval No. 12-2025/180-HC, 26 December 2025). 3. Results 3.1. Epidemiological and Demographic Characteristics From 2001 to 2025, 314 laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases were recorded in the five study units, a mean of 12.6 ± 18.4 cases per year (median 6; range 0–85). Most cases occurred in males (255; 81.2%) (Table 3). Case numbers fluctuated markedly (Figure 2). The largest outbreak occurred in 2005 (85 cases), followed by smaller peaks in 2003 (20), 2006 (20), and 2008 (30). After very low numbers in 2019–2023 (0–3 cases per year), cases rose sharply in 2024 (27) and 2025 (41). Regional incidence ranged from 0 to 1.70 per 100,000 in 2016–2023, increased to 3.88 per 100,000 in 2024, and reached an estimated 5.89 per 100,000 in 2025. Burlinsky District accounted for 44.9% of all cases and Baiterek District for 31.2% (Table 4), largely because of the 2005 outbreak, during which Burlinsky reported 54 cases. In the period with population data (2016–2025), however, Baiterek had the highest cumulative incidence (63.8 per 100,000), followed by Burlinsky (33.5), Chingirlau (14.3), Uralsk City (10.2), and Terekty (5.2). The resurgence in 2024–2025 was concentrated in Baiterek (22.7 and 22.2 per 100,000) and Burlinsky (12.2 and 15.8 per 100,000), with a rise in Uralsk City in 2025 (16 cases; 4.3 per 100,000). The single-year peak in Chingirlau (13.5 per 100,000 in 2017) reflected 2 cases in a small population (Figure 3). 3.2. Rodent Surveillance and Correlation Analysis The number of rodents examined per year ranged from 74 (2001) to 11,561 (2012) and was 1755 in 2024. Rodent hantavirus positivity declined from 1.95% in 2001–2005 to 0.18% in 2021–2025 (Table 2), including in 2024–2025, when human cases increased. For all four species, most captures occurred in autumn–winter (Figure S1). In 2002–2024, the mean percentage of annual captures obtained in spring–summer was 30.4% (range 7.0–59.3%) for M. glareolus, 42.2% (19.6–64.6%) for M. arvalis, 38.1% (21.0–61.5%) for A. uralensis, and 32.6% (10.6–69.1%) for M. musculus. In 2023 and 2024, spring–summer captures accounted for only 7.0% and 8.6% of annual M. glareolus captures. In contrast, 2024 was the only year in which most M. musculus captures (69.1%) occurred in spring–summer. The spring–summer percentage of M. musculus captures was positively correlated with district-level case counts (r = 0.32, p < 0.001; Table 5). The autumn–winter value is its complement and therefore shows the same coefficient with the opposite sign. The spring–summer percentages of the other species, including the bank vole, were not correlated with case counts. The number of antigen-positive rodents showed a weak, non-significant positive correlation (r = 0.18, p = 0.058). At the year level, human seroprevalence was not significantly correlated with case counts (r = −0.26, p = 0.50, n = 9 surveys in 2006–2024; r = 0.47, p = 0.17, n = 10 including 2025, when 41 of 150 persons tested were seropositive). 3.3. Regression Analysis Case counts were strongly overdispersed (mean 2.37, variance 36.6 per district-year; Poisson Pearson χ2/df = 4.08), and the NB dispersion parameter differed significantly from zero (α = 0.97; likelihood-ratio χ2 = 152.2, p < 0.001). In the linear panel specification, district effects were significant (F(4, 108) = 4.17, p = 0.003) and the Breusch–Pagan LM test indicated unobserved district heterogeneity (χ2 = 11.29, p < 0.001). There was no evidence of first-order serial correlation (Wooldridge F(1, 4) = 1.23, p = 0.33), but strong groupwise heteroskedasticity was present (modified Wald χ2(5) = 1227, p < 0.001), driven mainly by the large residual variance in Burlinsky District. Multicollinearity was negligible (VIF = 1.05) (Table 6). These results supported a count model with district fixed effects and robust standard errors as the primary analysis. In the primary NB model (Table 7), each one-percentage-point increase in the share of annual M. musculus captures obtained in spring–summer was associated with a 5.1% higher expected case count (IRR = 1.051; 95% CI: 1.024–1.080; p < 0.001). Each additional antigen-positive rodent was associated with a 0.9% higher expected count (IRR = 1.009; 95% CI: 1.003–1.016; p = 0.004). After adjustment, Burlinsky District did not differ significantly from Baiterek (IRR = 1.33; 95% CI: 0.76–2.35), whereas Uralsk City (IRR = 0.60), Chingirlau (IRR = 0.16), and Terekty (IRR = 0.04) had significantly lower case counts. The linear FE model gave consistent results (β for M. musculus = 0.129 additional cases per district-year per percentage point; 95% CI with year-clustered SEs: 0.014–0.245; p = 0.030) (Table S1). The model did not reproduce the magnitude of outbreak peaks (fitted 18.3 vs. 85 observed cases in 2005), indicating that other, unmeasured factors contributed to outbreak size. The association with M. musculus was robust in all sensitivity analyses (Table 8). In contrast, the association with rodent positivity disappeared when it was expressed as a percentage of rodents examined (IRR = 1.33 per percentage point; 95% CI: 0.56–3.13; p = 0.52), indicating that the association with the absolute number of positive animals largely reflected sampling effort. 4. papers.title_zh: 西哈萨克斯坦 肾综合征出血热 的生态相关因素与时空趋势:一项跨越25年的 One Health 监测研究(2001-2025)

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种在哈萨克斯坦西部受到公共卫生关注的啮齿动物传播的人畜共患病,但将人类与宿主监测联系起来的长期研究仍然稀缺。
analysis_zh.methods: 我们开展了一项回顾性纵向生态学研究,研究对象为西哈萨克斯坦地区五个区内实验室确诊的肾综合征出血热病例(2001-2025)及常规啮齿动物监测数据,采用负二项回归,加入区固定效应和按年聚类的稳健标准误(2002-2024;115 区年)。研究共检验了132,694只啮齿动物,其中1,083只(0.82%)为汉坦病毒抗原阳性。
analysis_zh.results: 总体共记录314例病例(男性占81.2%),2005年出现大规模爆发(85例),2024-2025年再次出现高发(27例和41例)。Burlinsky 区报告病例最多(44.9%),而 Baiterek 区在2016-2025年期间的发病率最高。春夏季 Mus musculus 捕获量占年捕获量的比例越高,病例数越多(发病率比 1.051 每百分点;95% 置信区间:1.024-1.080),即使排除爆发年份后结果仍稳健。正负抗原阳性啮齿动物数量与病例相关,但在按采样努力标准化后不再显著。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究展示了肾综合征出血热的长期生态相关性,并强调居住周边 Mus musculus 暴露的重要性,为流行地区的监测与风险评估提供了一体化健康框架。

papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10 , STAT1 , and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1 , BCL2 , and STAT 3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2 , MAPK3 , and TNF . Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host-pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the "One Health" framework.

papers.full_text: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization Simple Summary Hantaan virus, carried by rodents, causes severe bleeding and kidney disease in humans, making it a key concern for veterinary wildlife surveillance. Using computational methods, we studied early viral effects on human cells and screened for natural compounds. Three immune genes, CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10, were strongly activated early. Among six compounds, quercetin was most promising, with predicted good absorption and low toxicity. Further analysis indicated that quercetin may promote cell viability and suppress inflammation, thereby protecting cells from damage induced by HTNV infection. In baseline pharmacological assays using uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin at 3.9–7.8 μM was non-toxic, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted quercetin binds to the viral RNA polymerase at Lys884 and Arg892. These findings propose quercetin as a computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses. Abstract Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses, enveloped segmented negative-sense RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. They are predominantly maintained in rodent reservoir species, with which they have co-evolved a persistent, typically asymptomatic infection. Infected rodents do not manifest overt disease but sustain long-term viral carriage, with continuous shedding of infectious particles via excretory routes, namely urine, feces, and saliva. Human infection occurs through inhalation of virus-contaminated aerosols, direct contact with contaminated fomites or wounds, or, less frequently, via the digestive tract, leading to two severe clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS). Orthohantavirus hantaanense (Hantaan virus, HTNV) is the predominant etiological agent of HFRS in Asia, with reported case-fatality rates approaching 15%. Importantly, the occurrence of HTNV infection is not determined solely by viral or host factors. Human exposure is closely associated with the abundance, distribution, and infection status of rodent hosts, as well as the frequency of human–rodent contact. Rodent population dynamics and virus shedding are further influenced by environmental and ecological conditions, including climate variability, habitat characteristics, agricultural activities, and food availability and storage. Consequently, HTNV represents a typical One Health-related challenge in which viral maintenance in animals, environmental contamination, and human exposure are interconnected. Currently, no approved drug is available to break the aforementioned connection. Moreover, the clinical management of HTNV-infected cases still relies mainly on supportive treatment. In previous reports, ribavirin, a broad-spectrum nucleoside analog, has shown antiviral activity against hantaviruses and has been used in certain clinical settings. However, its therapeutic utility is limited by treatment timing and adverse effects, including hemolytic anemia and other treatment-related complications. Addressing these problems requires a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of HTNV and the exploration of potential drug candidates. After HTNV infection, on one hand, its own encoded proteins, such as nucleocapsid protein (NP) and glycoprotein (Gn/Gc), can inhibit the production of type I interferons by targeting the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling pathway, thereby suppressing the early warning system of the host’s innate immunity. In addition, NP can recruit and interact with fatty acid synthase (FASN), regulating lipid synthesis activity, providing necessary metabolic support for viral replication. On the other hand, HTNV infection can also activate the HIF-1 signaling pathway, aggravating barrier dysfunction and vascular leakage. Clinical studies have confirmed that the earlier the intervention is carried out for HTNV infection, the higher the cure rate for the patients. Therefore, identifying the targets of the early interaction between HTNV and the host and using these targets to explore potential candidate drugs is an effective way to address the one health-related threats posed by HTNV. By integrating omics results, compound databases, and computer-aided drug design, a systematic framework has been established to elucidate the interactions between bioactive compounds and complex biological networks. The framework integrating omics and computational drug design can not only discover antiviral drugs that protect humans, but also the host pathways it reveals may provide clues for understanding the persistence mechanism of pathogens in rodents. From the perspective of One Health, this means that intervention strategies can simultaneously address both “reducing human cases” and “understanding the maintenance mechanism of rodents”. For instance, Msobo et al. combined LC–MS-based metabolomics with network pharmacology to investigate the anti-SARS-CoV-2 potential of Salvia aurea and Salvia dolomitica, thereby identifying 83 phytochemicals predicted to interact strongly with multiple SARS-CoV-2-associated targets. Accordingly, the present study adopted a target-oriented strategy that integrates bioinformatics, network pharmacology, and molecular docking, together with preliminary in vitro transcriptomic and cytotoxicity assessments in uninfected cells, to generate hypotheses regarding natural compounds capable of modulating HTNV-related host responses. The overall workflow is illustrated in Figure 1. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Cells and Compound The HEK293T cell line was acquired from the China Center for Type Culture Collection. Quercetin (purity, 99.80%) was purchased from MedChemExpress (Cat. No. HY-18085). Quercetin was dissolved in DMSO to a stock concentration of 200 mM and stored at −80 °C. The final DMSO concentration in cell culture medium did not exceed 0.1% (v/v), and an equivalent DMSO vehicle control was included in all experiments. 2.2. Prediction of Therapeutic Candidate for Early-Stage HTNV Infection HTNV-related host interaction targets were collected from disease-related public databases and the GEO database. For public database mining, HTNV-related targets were retrieved from OMIM (, accessed on 9 June 2026), GeneCards (, accessed on 9 June 2026), and MalaCards (, accessed on 9 June 2026) using the keyword “Hantavirus” with species restricted to Homo sapiens. For transcriptomic data, the GSE89950 dataset profiling digital gene expression (DGE) in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) at 24 h post-exposure to HTNV components was retrieved from the GEO database. This dataset included three conditions (Mock, HTNV, and HTNV [Co60]), with one sample per condition. The processed per-gene DGE statistics (expression values, fold changes, and p-values) were obtained from the supplementary DGE result files of the GEO series. To verify these statistics, we additionally downloaded the raw tag-level data of GSE89950 (GSE89950_RAW.tar: GSM2393958_Mock, GSM2393959_HTNV, and GSM2393960_Co60). Independent processing of the raw tag data yielded 96,272, 84,715, and 85,736 unique tags (corresponding to 3.43, 3.40, and 3.44 million copies) in the Mock, HTNV, and HTNV(Co60) samples, respectively. After gene-level summarization, a total of 12,503 expressed genes were obtained, identical to the union of the gene-level supplementary files; the gene-level count matrix was verified to be exactly consistent with the raw tag data. We then re-derived the differential expression statistics for both comparisons in R using an exact binomial test under the Poisson model, with library-size proportions as the null expectation. The independently derived statistics were highly concordant with the supplementary files, confirming the reliability of the DEG lists retrieved from GEO. Given the lack of biological replicates, DEG analysis was performed as an exploratory screening, and nominal p-values were reported without Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. DEGs were screened from the HTNV(Co60)_vs_Control and HTNV_vs_Control comparisons using thresholds of nominal p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0. Targets retrieved from public databases were imported into the STRING database () to construct a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, with a confidence score > 0.4 as the cutoff. Topological analysis was performed using the CytoNCA plugin in Cytoscape (version 3.9.1) to screen for core targets based on degree centrality (DC), betweenness centrality (BC), eigenvector centrality (EC), and closeness centrality (CC). Venn diagram analysis was used to identify the overlap between public database targets and DEGs from the HTNV (Co60)_vs_Control comparison. These core targets were then imported into the HERB database () for compound matching. Venn analysis was applied to the resulting compounds to screen for natural compounds predicted to interact with these core targets. 2.3. Prediction of Toxicity, Drug-Likeness, and Oral Bioavailability of Candidate Compounds SMILES notations for each compound were obtained from the PubChem database (, accessed on 1 July 2026). Organ toxicity (with 0.5 set as the threshold), toxicity endpoints, and metabolic characteristics were predicted using ProTox-II (, accessed on 20 June 2026). Interactions between each compound and six major cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4) were evaluated using a 0–1 scoring system. Drug-likeness (based on Lipinski, Ghose, Veber, Egan, and Muegge rules), bioavailability scores, and gastrointestinal (GI) absorption were predicted using SwissADME (, accessed on 20 June 2026). 2.4. Analysis of the Potential Targets of Quercetin in the Treatment of HTNV Infection Quercetin-related targets were retrieved from public databases [TCMSP (, accessed on 20 June 2026), SwissTargetPrediction (, accessed on 20 June 2026), and HERB (, accessed on 20 June 2026)] and the GEO database. The gene expression profiles of GSE167391 were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. This dataset included nine samples divided into three groups: normal control HUVECs (Control_1–3), ox-LDL-injured HUVECs (Ox_ldl_1–3), and quercetin-pretreated ox-LDL-injured HUVECs (Quercetin_1–3). Transcript-level FPKM values were aggregated to the gene level by summing isoforms, and genes with a mean FPKM ≥ 1 in at least one group (n = 3 per group) were retained. Because FPKM values are normalized continuous expression estimates that violate the count-based negative binomial assumption of DESeq2 and are likewise unsuitable for voom, the data were treated as microarray-like and analyzed with limma in R (v4.3.2). FPKM values were log2-transformed with a pseudocount of 1 and quantile-normalized. A linear model was fitted with the design~0 + group. Comparisons were made between Ox-ldl vs. Control and Quercetin_Ox-ldl vs. Control. Genes with an adjusted p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg) < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0 were considered differentially expressed. Venn analysis was then applied to intersect the DEGs from these comparisons with the quercetin-related targets, thereby identifying the potential targets of quercetin in the intervention against HTNV infection. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the targets was performed using the DAVID (, accessed on 20 August 2026). 2.5. Baseline Pharmacological Characterization of Candidate Compounds in Uninfected Cells To evaluate the potential of quercetin to protect cell proliferation, we integrated target data from online databases with quercetin-related targets identified from our transcriptomic analysis. A protein–protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using the STRING database, and four topological parameters, namely degree centrality (DC), betweenness centrality (BC), closeness centrality (CC), and eigenvector centrality (EC), were calculated with the CytoNCA plugin in Cytoscape 3.9.1. KEGG pathway and Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analyses were performed using DAVID (, accessed on 20 June 2026), and the enriched terms were ranked to identify the core functional pathways associated with the hub targets. Molecular docking of quercetin with the top-ranked targets was conducted using CB-Dock2 (, accessed on 22 July 2026). For in vitro validation, the initial concentration of quercetin was prepared at 1000 μM, and 10 concentration gradients were generated through a twofold dilution method. HEK293T cells were inoculated in 12-well plates and 96-well plates, respectively, and then treated with the dilution solution for 48 h. The cell viability in the 96-well plate was determined by the CCK-8 method. The experiment was repeated 8 times. Total RNA was extracted from the cells in the 12-well plates according to the instructions of the test kit (RM201, Vazyme, Nanjing, China), and the expression levels of related genes (STAT3, BCL2, MAPK3 and TNF) were detected using the RT-qPCR method (R323-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) with the 2−ΔΔCt method. All reaction systems and reaction temperatures were carried out in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Each group was repeated with 3 biological replicates. β-Actin was used as the reference gene. The primer sequences are shown in Supplementary Materials. 2.6. Evaluation of Candidate Compound Intervention Against Viral RdRp Proteins The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) protein sequences of Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) were retrieved from the NCBI database (accession numbers: ALI59821.1 for HTNV and UYS55322.1 for SEOV). Sequence alignment was performed using DNAMAN software (version 5.0). Three-dimensional structural models of the HTNV and SEOV RdRp proteins were subsequently generated using SWISS-MODEL (, accessed on 3 June 2026). To investigate quercetin-binding residues in HTNV more precisely, the crystal structure of HTNV RdRp (PDB ID: 8P1L) was retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Molecular docking of these protein structures with quercetin was performed using CB-Dock2, and the interacting residues were identified and analyzed. The functional significance of the docking residues was further evaluated through Venn analysis. 2.7. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9.5). For RT-qPCR data, comparisons among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Unpaired Student’s t-test was used for two-group comparisons. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. 3. Results 3.1. Identification of Candidate Compounds The workflow for candidate compound screening is illustrated in Figure 2A. Restricting the analysis to Homo sapiens yielded 96 HTNV-associated targets from online public databases. The sources of target acquisition are shown in Table 1. Topological analysis of the PPI network using multiple algorithms in Cytoscape 3.9.1 identified STAT1, IFNG, IL6, TNF, IL10, and CXCL10 as the six highest-ranked core genes (Figure 2B). Host transcriptional responses were profiled using the GSE89950 dataset from GEO, which captures gene expression in HUVECs treated with HTNV components. full_text_sections.full_text: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization Simple Summary Hantaan virus, carried by rodents, causes severe bleeding and kidney disease in humans, making it a key concern for veterinary wildlife surveillance. Using computational methods, we studied early viral effects on human cells and screened for natural compounds. Three immune genes, CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10, were strongly activated early. Among six compounds, quercetin was most promising, with predicted good absorption and low toxicity. Further analysis indicated that quercetin may promote cell viability and suppress inflammation, thereby protecting cells from damage induced by HTNV infection. In baseline pharmacological assays using uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin at 3.9–7.8 μM was non-toxic, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted quercetin binds to the viral RNA polymerase at Lys884 and Arg892. These findings propose quercetin as a computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses. Abstract Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses, enveloped segmented negative-sense RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. They are predominantly maintained in rodent reservoir species, with which they have co-evolved a persistent, typically asymptomatic infection. Infected rodents do not manifest overt disease but sustain long-term viral carriage, with continuous shedding of infectious particles via excretory routes, namely urine, feces, and saliva. Human infection occurs through inhalation of virus-contaminated aerosols, direct contact with contaminated fomites or wounds, or, less frequently, via the digestive tract, leading to two severe clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS). Orthohantavirus hantaanense (Hantaan virus, HTNV) is the predominant etiological agent of HFRS in Asia, with reported case-fatality rates approaching 15%. Importantly, the occurrence of HTNV infection is not determined solely by viral or host factors. Human exposure is closely associated with the abundance, distribution, and infection status of rodent hosts, as well as the frequency of human–rodent contact. Rodent population dynamics and virus shedding are further influenced by environmental and ecological conditions, including climate variability, habitat characteristics, agricultural activities, and food availability and storage. Consequently, HTNV represents a typical One Health-related challenge in which viral maintenance in animals, environmental contamination, and human exposure are interconnected. Currently, no approved drug is available to break the aforementioned connection. Moreover, the clinical management of HTNV-infected cases still relies mainly on supportive treatment. In previous reports, ribavirin, a broad-spectrum nucleoside analog, has shown antiviral activity against hantaviruses and has been used in certain clinical settings. However, its therapeutic utility is limited by treatment timing and adverse effects, including hemolytic anemia and other treatment-related complications. Addressing these problems requires a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of HTNV and the exploration of potential drug candidates. After HTNV infection, on one hand, its own encoded proteins, such as nucleocapsid protein (NP) and glycoprotein (Gn/Gc), can inhibit the production of type I interferons by targeting the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling pathway, thereby suppressing the early warning system of the host’s innate immunity. In addition, NP can recruit and interact with fatty acid synthase (FASN), regulating lipid synthesis activity, providing necessary metabolic support for viral replication. On the other hand, HTNV infection can also activate the HIF-1 signaling pathway, aggravating barrier dysfunction and vascular leakage. Clinical studies have confirmed that the earlier the intervention is carried out for HTNV infection, the higher the cure rate for the patients. Therefore, identifying the targets of the early interaction between HTNV and the host and using these targets to explore potential candidate drugs is an effective way to address the one health-related threats posed by HTNV. By integrating omics results, compound databases, and computer-aided drug design, a systematic framework has been established to elucidate the interactions between bioactive compounds and complex biological networks. The framework integrating omics and computational drug design can not only discover antiviral drugs that protect humans, but also the host pathways it reveals may provide clues for understanding the persistence mechanism of pathogens in rodents. From the perspective of One Health, this means that intervention strategies can simultaneously address both “reducing human cases” and “understanding the maintenance mechanism of rodents”. For instance, Msobo et al. combined LC–MS-based metabolomics with network pharmacology to investigate the anti-SARS-CoV-2 potential of Salvia aurea and Salvia dolomitica, thereby identifying 83 phytochemicals predicted to interact strongly with multiple SARS-CoV-2-associated targets. Accordingly, the present study adopted a target-oriented strategy that integrates bioinformatics, network pharmacology, and molecular docking, together with preliminary in vitro transcriptomic and cytotoxicity assessments in uninfected cells, to generate hypotheses regarding natural compounds capable of modulating HTNV-related host respon…

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen mainly distributed in East Asia that causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans, exemplifying a One Health challenge.
analysis.methods: An integrated bioinformatics workflow—including early‑stage host transcriptomic analysis, network pharmacology screening of natural compounds, molecular docking, and baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells—was employed to identify host interaction factors and predict therapeutic mechanisms.
analysis.results: CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were the principal up‑regulated core genes; six candidate natural compounds were retrieved, with quercetin emerging as the most promising due to predicted high gastrointestinal absorption and acceptable toxicity; network analyses suggested quercetin may regulate apoptosis‑related targets (AKT1, BCL2, STAT3) and mitigate HTNV‑induced damage; in HEK293T cells quercetin showed low cytotoxicity at 3.90625–7.8125 µM, increased cell viability and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3 and TNF; docking predicted favorable binding to HTNV RNA‑dependent RNA polymerase at Lys884 and Arg892.
analysis.contribution: The study proposes quercetin as a hypothesis‑generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV‑related host responses and offers a framework to generate mechanistic hypotheses that can aid surveillance, prevention and control of HTNV within a One Health context.
analysis.limitations: Findings are limited to computational predictions and baseline assays in uninfected cells, with no experimental validation in infected models or in vivo systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen mainly in East Asia that causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, a One Health challenge. Methods: An integrated bioinformatics workflow—early‑stage host transcriptomics, network pharmacology screening, molecular docking, and baseline assays in uninfected HEK293T cells—identified host interaction factors and candidate compounds. Results: CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were top up‑regulated genes; six natural compounds were screened, with quercetin highlighted for high predicted absorption and low toxicity; network analysis linked quercetin to apoptosis‑related targets (AKT1, BCL2, STAT3); quercetin showed low cytotoxicity at 3.9–7.8 µM, increased viability and reduced BCL2, MAPK3, TNF transcription; docking predicted binding to HTNV RdRp (Lys884, Arg892). Contribution: The work proposes quercetin as a hypothesis‑generating candidate and provides a computational framework to support HTNV surveillance and control within One Health. Limitations: Results are based on in silico predictions and baseline assays in uninfected cells, lacking experimental validation in infected or in vivo models.

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒(HTNV)是一种主要分布于东亚的啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,可导致人类严重的肾综合征出血热,体现了One Health挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用一套集成的生物信息学工作流——包括早期宿主转录组分析、天然化合物网络药理学筛选、分子对接以及在未感染的HEK293T细胞中的基础药理学实验——以识别宿主相互作用因子并预测治疗机制。
analysis_zh.results: CXCL10、STAT1和IL10为主要上调的核心基因;检索到六种候选天然化合物,其中槲皮素因预测的高胃肠吸收率和可接受的毒性而最具潜力;网络分析提示槲皮素可能调控凋亡相关靶点(AKT1、BCL2、STAT3)并减轻HTNV诱导的损伤;在HEK293T细胞中,槲皮素在3.90625–7.8125 μM浓度下表现出低细胞毒性,提升细胞活力并降低BCL2、MAPK3和TNF的转录水平;对接预测其在Lys884和Arg892位点与HTNV RNA依赖性RNA聚合酶形成有利结合。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提出槲皮素作为一种用于调节HTNV相关宿主反应的假设生成式计算候选药物,并提供了一个生成机制假设的框架,可帮助在One Health背景下对HTNV进行监测、预防和控制。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果仅限于计算预测和未感染细胞的基础实验,缺乏在感染模型或体内系统中的实验验证。
